task: What does a valid WebMCP Challenge submission have to include? List all deliverables and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository.
answer: A valid submission must include four deliverables: (1) a working live URL accessible to judges in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or in Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled; authenticated apps are allowed, with credentials supplied in the Submission Form; (2) a text project description explaining why the use case strongly fits WebMCP, how it improves user experience, what people and agents can do together that was previously difficult or impossible, and briefly how WebMCP was implemented; (3) a public YouTube demo video under 3 minutes, with audio, clearly showing both what was built and how WebMCP was used; and (4) a public GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repository containing all source code, assets, and instructions needed to make the project functional, plus an open-source license file that is detectable and visible at the top of the repository page/About section. The submission page also shows the expected WebMCP tool-registration pattern in the repository guidance.

task: Can a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualify? Explain which work counts, how judges assess it, and what evidence the entrant must provide.
answer: Yes. A project that existed before the submission period began on August 25, 2026 can qualify only if it was meaningfully extended with WebMCP after the submission period started. Judges evaluate a pre-existing project solely on the work added during the submission period, not on its earlier functionality. The entrant must clearly distinguish old work from new work and provide evidence that the WebMCP extension occurred within the period—for example, timestamped or dated commit history, or equivalent documentation.

task: Give the final extended submission deadline in PT and in EDT. Explain why it changed and identify the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close.
answer: The final extended deadline is Friday, September 4, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. PT, which is 4:00 a.m. EDT. It was moved 12 hours later from Thursday, September 3 at 1:00 p.m. PT because of an ongoing outage that the OpenAI team was working to fix. Once submissions close, entrants must not change the source-code repository, demo video, or live site/application; the live site must also remain online and the video must not be swapped.

task: How do the two judging stages work? Name all four equally weighted criteria in the second stage and explain the tie-breaking order.
answer: Stage One is a pass/fail viability screen: the project must reasonably fit the challenge theme and reasonably use the required APIs/SDKs. Every submission that passes advances to Stage Two, where judges score four equally weighted criteria: (1) WebMCP Leverage—depth and skill of WebMCP use, genuine effort, and a working non-trivial implementation; (2) Execution—a working/runnable, complete and coherent product experience rather than only a technical proof of concept; (3) Potential Impact—a credible, specific real problem and audience, with the demonstrated solution actually addressing it; and (4) Creativity & Ambition—novelty, creativity, and differentiation from existing concepts. For a tie, compare tied entries on the criteria in that listed order: first WebMCP Leverage, then Execution, then Potential Impact, then Creativity & Ambition. If still tied on all four, the judging panel votes.

task: How can judges test a submitted application in each supported browser environment? Include the minimum Chrome version and required flag, whether judges must open the live application, and where an entrant must provide private login credentials.
answer: Judges can test the live application in either (1) ChatGPT’s in-app browser, where WebMCP works by default, or (2) Google Chrome 149 or later after enabling chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and restarting Chrome. Entrants must provide a working live URL that functions in those environments and clear testing instructions. Judges are not required to build the project from source, and they are not generally required to test it, but the submission FAQ says they will visit/open the live URL directly to see how it works. A live app may be private/authenticated, but the entrant must put the necessary login credentials in the Devpost Submission Form (with the testing instructions) so judges can access it.
